R is a language for statistical computing and graphics - it is great for working
with data.

This tutorial assumes users have some experience coding.  Below are the software
requirement for this tutorial:
*An installation of R. 
*An Integrated Development Environment (IDE), like RStudio or Positron. 
*Alternatively, access to a cloud-based IDE, such as Posit Cloud. 

## Packages
```{r, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
```

## Reading Data in from the API
To read in the datasets via the API, we are using the `sf` package to do this since 
they are spatial datasets, but `jsonlite` is also a great package for reading in 
JSONs.If preferred, the datasets can also be downloaded manually and the same 
analysis can be performed. 

```{r, message=FALSE}
vacant <- st_read("https://services6.arcgis.com/bdPqSfflsdgFRVVM/arcgis/rest/services/Vacant_Properties/FeatureServer/0/query?outFields=*&where=1%3D1&f=geojson")

zip <- st_read("https://services6.arcgis.com/bdPqSfflsdgFRVVM/arcgis/rest/services/Syracuse_Zip_Codes_2022_View/FeatureServer/0/query?outFields=*&where=1%3D1&f=geojson")
```

## Grabbing Counts
In the chunk below, `count` is being used to create a dataframe that shows the number
of vacant properties per zip code. 

`st_drop_geometry` removes the geometry from the the vacant properties data, since 
the goal is to map the number of vacant properties in each zip code within the City,
rather than mapping each individual point. 

```{r}
counts <- count(st_drop_geometry(vacant), Zip)
head(counts)
```
## Joining 
Next, the `counts` dataframe is being joined to the zip code polygons.
```{r}
zips_joined <- left_join(zip, counts, by =(c("ZIP" = "Zip")))
```

## Mapping
```{r}
ggplot(zips_joined) + 
  geom_sf(aes(fill = n), color = "white") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "mako", direction = -1, na.value = "grey40") +
  labs(title="Vacant Properties by Zip Code in Syracuse, NY", 
       fill = "Count of Vacant \nProperties") + 
  theme_void()
```
